status_research.rationale: I read the held EO 10156 (15 FR 5789, Aug. 26, 1950; the held extract begins with neighbouring railroad-list pages and carries an unrelated sugar regulation after the order). Para. 1 designates the Under Secretary (1(a)), then the ranking Assistant Secretary (1(b)), then the Solicitor (1(c)) to perform the duties of the Secretary of the Interior in case of death, resignation, absence or sickness; para. 2 defines the ranking Assistant Secretary; para. 3 supersedes EO 9866. It has no own term or sunset. I read the held full text of EO 10753 (23 FR 1107, Feb. 15, 1958): it sets a new order of succession (Under Secretary; Assistant Secretaries and the Assistant Secretary for Fish and Wildlife; Solicitor) and closes with 'This order supersedes Executive Order No. 10156 of August 26, 1950, entitled Designation of Certain Officers of the Department of the Interior to Act as Secretary of the Interior.' That names the whole order by number and title, covers every paragraph, and has no savings or exception clause, so the whole of EO 10156 ended no later than Feb. 15, 1958. D6 self-check: the only later event in the history is EO 10753 (the catalog 'Superseded by: EO 10753'). No held instrument other than EO 10753 names EO 10156 (hits for the number in EO_10155, EO_10407, EO_9599 and EO_13825 are page numbers or an index line). EO 10753 was itself superseded by EO 11487 (Oct. 6, 1969), sec. 2, which I read; it names only EO 10753 and does not name, restore or revive EO 10156, so the supersession of EO 10156 stands. No earlier end by a term, condition or amendment appears. The catalog note and the 1989 snapshot agree but are leads only. Provisional NO hypothesis; the effective end is not adjudicated beyond 'on or before Feb. 15, 1958'.

Held EO 10753 (23 FR 1107, Feb. 15, 1958) prescribes a complete new succession list and states 'This order supersedes Executive Order No. 10156 of August 26, 1950', by number, date and title, with no savings clause. A full replacement of a succession order ends the whole of it: my independent status NO, agreeing with the producer. Refutation attempts: right instrument and quoted sentence verified; whole scope (EO 10753 covers the entire subject); no own term ending earlier. D6: was any later event that ended or changed this clause removed or ignored? No. The history has only the EO 10753 events (catalog 'Superseded by' and 'Supersedes'); held-text hits for '10156' in EO_10155, EO_10407, EO_9599 and EO_13825 are a table/index line or page numbers; EO 11487 sec. 2 later supersedes EO 10753 only and revives nothing. Accept as a provisional NO hypothesis (end on or before Feb. 15, 1958).

versions.research_rationale:
Executive Order 10156 (15 FR 5789 (Federal Register of August 29, 1950)) was signed August 26, 1950. The held text begins with unrelated railroad-list pages of the same Federal Register issue and carries an unrelated sugar regulation after the order; the dossier's clause covered the railroad list's table fragments, so the inventory is corrected to the order's own text. The order designates, under section 179 of the Revised Statutes, the officers who perform the duties of the Secretary of the Interior in case of death, resignation, absence or sickness: the Under Secretary (1(a)), then the ranking Assistant Secretary (1(b)), then the Solicitor (1(c)); paragraph 2 defines the ranking Assistant Secretary; paragraph 3 supersedes Executive Order No. 9866 of June 14, 1947. On 2026-10-14 the designations in paragraphs 1 and 2 are terminated by Executive Order 10753 (23 FR 1107 (Federal Register of February 20, 1958)), signed February 15, 1958 by President Eisenhower, which sets a new order of succession and closes with the sentence “This order supersedes Executive Order” naming Executive Order No. 10156 of August 26, 1950 and its title. That sentence names this order by number and date and has no exception or saving clause. Paragraph 3 was a one-time supersession performed when the order took effect and is terminated on August 26, 1950. The order has no own-terms sunset. The only later instrument in the held corpus that names the order is Executive Order 10753 (the neighbouring Federal Register page of Executive Order 10155 reprints this order's heading, not a later instrument). The Federal Register disposition-note search lists the one hit, Executive Order 10753; the U.S. Code and eCFR citation searches report no hit. The superseded Executive Order No. 9866 stays superseded; that is a surviving consequence of paragraph 3 and not a command left to end.

Executive Order 10753 says it supersedes this order and gives no separate effective date, so the supersession took effect when signed on February 15, 1958; the Federal Register page shows it was filed February 18, 1958, which is disclosed as the alternative if effectiveness is tied to filing. Paragraph 3's supersession of Executive Order No. 9866 was exhausted by performance on August 26, 1950, the signing date, which the order's own text supports because it states no other effective date.","independent_command_check":"Paragraph 3 is an independent one-time command performed at signing. Paragraphs 1 and 2 are a continuing standing designation; paragraph 2 depends on paragraph 1(b) and has no independent duration.","savings_check":"The supersession of Executive Order No. 9866 in paragraph 3 is a performed act whose consequence survives (that earlier order stays superseded). The designations in paragraphs 1 and 2 left nothing accrued once Executive Order 10753 replaced them; neither the order nor Executive Order 10753 contains a saving clause for acts under the earlier designation.","scope_check":"Three operative pieces: paragraph 1 with its three designations (the order's lead and subparagraphs (a) to (c)), paragraph 2 (who counts as the ranking Assistant Secretary), and paragraph 3 (supersession of Executive Order No. 9866). Paragraph 2 operates only for the purposes of paragraph 1(b), so it ends with paragraph 1."}

savings_residuals.reason: The supersession of Executive Order No. 9866 in paragraph 3 is a performed act whose consequence survives (that earlier order stays superseded). The designations in paragraphs 1 and 2 left nothing accrued once Executive Order 10753 replaced them; neither the order nor Executive Order 10753 contains a saving clause for acts under the earlier designation.
